statement: Cards numbered 1 to 30 are in a bag. Cards are taken out without looking and kept. What is the smallest number of cards that must be taken out to be certain that two of the numbers taken have a product that is a multiple of 6?

choices.misconception: I kept only the numbers that are neither even nor multiples of 3, which gave a safe set of 10, and added one.
I built my safe set from the odd multiples of 3 instead of the even numbers that are not multiples of 3, so it had only 15 numbers.
I found the largest set of 20 numbers with no such pair and gave that, instead of one more.
I forgot that a multiple of 6 times any number is a multiple of 6, so I let all five multiples of 6 into my safe set of 25.

hints: Sort 1 to 30 by divisibility: by 2, by 3, by both, or neither.
Find the largest collection of numbers in which no two have a product divisible by 6, then add one. A product is a multiple of 6 when, between them, the two numbers supply a factor 2 and a factor 3.

A multiple of 6 clashes with everything. An even number that is not a multiple of 3 clashes with an odd multiple of 3. Count each group: 5 multiples of 6, 10 other even numbers, 5 odd multiples of 3, 10 of neither kind.

solutions.reliable: Split 1 to 30 into four groups: multiples of 6 (5 numbers), even numbers that are not multiples of 3 (10 numbers), odd multiples of 3 (5 numbers) and numbers divisible by neither 2 nor 3 (10 numbers). A multiple of 6 times any number is a multiple of 6, so a safe collection with more than one number contains no multiple of 6. An even number times an odd multiple of 3 is a multiple of 6, so a safe collection cannot use both of those groups. The biggest safe collection is the 10 numbers of neither kind plus the 10 even non-multiples of 3, which is 20 numbers, and it really is safe because none of its products has a factor 3. So 20 cards can avoid it and 21 cannot. The transferable idea: the answer to a 'must be certain' question is the largest safe collection plus one, so find exactly which groups clash.

whyOnTest: Pigeonhole questions test the full argument: build the biggest set that avoids the event, then add one, and each step has its own trap among the choices.
